examples.prompt: The new Delegation wording is in delegation.md, and AGENTS.md has an older one I edited. Update it.
examples.result: The skill runs `classify` on the offered wording, the section found in AGENTS.md, and the retired wordings. For a part marked `update` it recommends the merged text, with your own sentences kept. It writes nothing until you approve.

examples.prompt: Both the new wording and my edit changed the same sentence.
examples.result: The part is a `conflict`. The skill shows the base, found, and offered sentences that collide, recommends a resolution it marks as decided with its reason, and asks you to choose.
The skill runs `load release-checklist` and prints the document that answers the name. It reads nothing from tier folders itself.
The skill runs `list` and reports each name with its description, and its status when it is not found. For which contribution of each is used, it runs `list --trace`.

examples.prompt: Find a reference about commit messages.
examples.result: The skill runs `search` with the topic and names the best matches. When nothing matches it says so and does not guess a name.

examples.prompt: Create a repo reference called release-checklist.
examples.result: The skill runs `create release-checklist --dry-run`, shows you the target path and the content, and writes the file under `.agents/references/` only after you approve. It then runs `load release-checklist --trace` and confirms the new file is `used`.

examples.prompt: Change what the commit-style reference says, just for me.
examples.result: The skill writes a contribution in `~/.agents/references/` holding only the sections you change. It patches the document below by default, so the sections you leave out are kept. It never edits a contribution a plugin ships.

examples.prompt: Two plugins ship project-tracker.capabilities.github. Use repobuddy's.
examples.result: The skill runs `customize project-tracker.capabilities.github --extends repobuddy`, which writes the selection to `.agents/references/` after you approve, then confirms the name loads.

examples.prompt: Make release-checklist ask for a changelog entry, just for this repo.
examples.result: The skill runs `customize release-checklist --base` to read what the name builds to, drafts a body from your request, and shows it. After you approve, it writes it with `--request` and `--body`, recording the picks, sources, and your request, so a changed source plugin shows up later as a `reference-stale` warning.

examples.prompt: Delete my project contribution to release-checklist.
examples.result: The skill runs `delete release-checklist --dry-run`, shows the file and what answers the name afterwards, and deletes only after you approve.

examples.prompt: Load reported reference-legacy-format. Fix my reference files.
examples.result: The skill runs `migrate` and shows every change it would make, saying which files are in your home folder, where no git history restores them. After you approve, it runs `migrate --write`, then `check`, and reports anything left.

The skill runs `load commit-style --trace` and reports the stack, the contributions behind each section with the operation each applied, and each layer that was `shadowed`, `not used`, or `not read`, with its reason.

cli.$run:
Install the package, or run it once with `npx`. The `reference` skill runs the same command from a launcher bundled in the plugin.

```sh
npm install --save-dev cyber-agentkit
npx cyber-agentkit reference list

# or, without installing
npx -y cyber-agentkit reference list
```
cli.$format: `load`, `create`, `customize`, and `delete` answer in `text` unless `--format` says otherwise. The other subcommands answer in `toon`, a compact format an agent reads. Pass `--format json` to pipe the answer. Each command prints only the fields that answer it. A command that cannot complete (exit 1) or was called wrongly (exit 2) prints one error value on stdout with a stable `code`; a command that answered, including `load` for a name not found and a failing `check`, exits 0. Warnings go to stderr as `warning: <code>: <message>`.

examples.title: Print one reference.
examples.explain: The document prints as it is composed, without frontmatter.

examples.title: Give the status and composed frontmatter.
examples.explain: `--metadata` makes the entry a record with its `status` and `metadata`. Without it, a found name is its content alone.

examples.title: Report how a name was built.
examples.explain: `--trace` writes a summary line, each section with the contributions behind it, and every layer checked with its outcome. It goes to stderr in `text` format, so this page shows only the document; run it to see the trace.

examples.title: Keep only names that match a pattern.
examples.explain: `*` stands for any run of characters; the rest must match exactly.

examples.title: See where a customization is written.
examples.explain: Each place says who it reaches, and the heading paths of the document below it, which a section of the new file can match.

examples.title: Preview a new reference without writing it.
examples.explain: Nothing is written. Run it again without `--dry-run` to create the file.

examples.title: Preview a delete.
examples.explain: The report names the file and what answers the name afterwards.

examples.title: List the implementations of an interface.
examples.explain: Each implementation comes with its pin, description, and the sections it does not support.

examples.title: Check every reference.
examples.explain: The answer gives the failures, if any, the warnings passed on, and the count that pass. The command exits 0 when it answered, even when a check fails.

examples.title: Print the plan.
examples.explain: Nothing is written. Each row gives a file in a version 1 form, or under a name a plugin renamed, and what it becomes.

examples.title: Apply it.
examples.explain: Every change that is not manual is made, and the same plan is printed.

examples.title: Pick what a name builds on.
examples.explain: The report gives the target path and the selection it would write. Run it again without `--dry-run` to write it.

examples.title: Print what a generator reads.
examples.explain: Nothing is written. The output is the name resolved with your picks, which a body written from a request builds on.
